statement: In 142 healthy adults with little drug experience and no psychiatric history who took LSD and/or psilocybin in six placebo-controlled laboratory trials in Switzerland (Müller et al., 2022), 13 (9.2%) described flashback-like experiences when asked at the end of the study: 7 of 90 after LSD only, 2 of 24 after psilocybin only and 4 of 28 after both. They were mostly single, brief visual changes lasting seconds to minutes, mostly in the days right after the last session, and 10 of the 13 felt neutral or pleasant; 2 people (1.4%) found them distressing, one of whom went on to have panic attacks and left the study, and one person had brief visual flashbacks, which she felt as positive, on and off for seven months. No one reported problems in daily life and no one was found to meet the criteria for hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD); with no case among 142 people, a true rate of up to about 2% cannot be ruled out (editors' calculation). There was no comparison with how often similar experiences happen without a drug, and the participants were screened volunteers, so rates in recreational use may differ. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: About 1 in 11 healthy volunteers who took LSD or psilocybin in lab studies said they later had a flashback, usually a short change in what they saw, in the days after. Most did not mind it; 2 of 142 were upset by it. Nobody developed lasting vision problems. These were careful lab studies with screened people, so it may be different in everyday use.
population: Healthy adults aged 25 to 65 with little previous drug use and no personal or family psychiatric history, in six placebo-controlled crossover trials in Basel (142 people, 74 women)
exposure: LSD and/or psilocybin given in the trials
comparator: None for the flashback outcome (frequencies are descriptive)
outcome: Flashback phenomena reported at the end-of-study visit and at follow-up; DSM-5 hallucinogen persisting perception disorder
magnitude: 13 of 142 (9.2%): LSD only 7 of 90 (7.8%), psilocybin only 2 of 24 (8.3%), both 4 of 28 (14.3%); distressing 2 of 142 (1.4%); HPPD 0 of 142 (editors' calculation: one-sided 95% upper limit about 2.1%). Mostly visual (11 of 13), seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%); single occurrence in 53.8%.

statement: In 24 healthy adults with previous LSD experience given a single low laboratory dose of LSD and, on another day, a placebo (one randomized, double-blind crossover study in Brazil; Wiessner et al., 2022), the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD changes thinking the next morning. In models adjusted for body mass index and time since last psychedelic use, people recalled a complex drawing and card locations somewhat better and named more words beginning with a given letter after LSD than after placebo, but did worse on a card-sorting test of mental flexibility (fewer categories completed, more errors and repeated wrong answers), with partial eta squared from 0.19 to 0.34; attention, self-control, reasoning, word-list memory and drawing fluency did not differ. About 66 test scores were analysed without correction for multiple testing, the authors report that the unadjusted analyses showed few differences, practice effects were large, the paper's text and table disagree on the direction of two card-sorting scores, and a few people account for much of the card-sorting difference in the figure. The study did not measure mood or sleep. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Twenty-four people who had taken LSD before took a small dose in a lab, and a dummy drink on another day. The next morning they did memory, word and puzzle tests. After LSD, a few memory and word scores were a little better and one card-sorting puzzle was a little worse than after the dummy drink. These small differences may be chance, because many scores were checked. Mood and sleep were not measured.
population: Healthy adults aged 25 to 61 (8 of 24 women) with at least one previous LSD experience and no psychiatric illness, in a laboratory study in Campinas, Brazil
exposure: A single low oral dose of LSD given by researchers in the morning (amount and timing are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people after an inactive placebo in a separate session two weeks apart
outcome: Performance on memory, fluency, mental flexibility, attention, inhibition and reasoning tests the next morning

statement: In 213 healthy volunteers aged 25 to 64 (108 women) who took LSD mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present (some sessions included an MRI scan), and placebo on another day in eight of the nine studies (nine double-blind crossover studies pooled by the Basel laboratory that ran them, 297 LSD sessions; one dose by mouth per session, 25 to 200 micrograms, as study conditions; Vizeli et al., 2024), the dose given was the strongest predictor of almost every effect compared with placebo, and characteristics measured before the dose were also associated with the response at a given dose: higher well-being rated just before, with stronger subjective effects in general, by the Discussion's summary (it was significantly associated with every self-rated scale, the anxiety-type scales included, except a bad drug effect and two others; the direction scale by scale is shown only in a figure not read); anxiety rated just before, with more anxiety during the session; openness, with more mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion, with more visual and auditory changes; more previous hallucinogen experience, with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; and genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with higher blood levels of LSD and more anxious ego dissolution. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any effect. Older age went with more, and higher body weight with less, bad drug effect, and women had smaller increases than men in four positive ratings and in body temperature; women's slightly less positive ratings were not significant when one dose per study was analysed (the text does not say whether the temperature difference held), and the abstract's statement that sex and body weight had no significant influence does not match the main results. The text gives the direction and significance of each association after correction for 551 tests but no sizes, which are only in a figure and a supplement not read here, so how much any characteristic other than dose matters cannot be said; bad drug effects were generally small. Expectations were not among the 19 predictors, and the setting barely varied. Genes for the CYP2D6 enzyme and earlier hallucinogen use went with feeling more or less from the same amount; earlier use was compared between people, so it cannot show that use itself changed the response. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy adults, the LSD dose was linked most closely to how strong the effects were. People who felt well just before had stronger effects, people who felt anxious had more anxiety, open personalities had more mystical feelings, and people who had used hallucinogens more often had a smaller overall effect. The paper gives the direction of each link but not its size. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

exposure: Characteristics measured before dosing: dose, mood just before the dose, personality, previous hallucinogen experience, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, age, sex and body weight; whether the session included an MRI scan
comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at a given dose (placebo sessions in the same people in eight of nine studies)
outcome: Self-rated effects relative to placebo (visual analogue scales, 5D-ASC, MEQ30), blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and blood LSD level
magnitude: Directions and corrected significance only; no sizes in the text. Dose strongest for every effect except body temperature (selected by LASSO for all 29 responses, largest for 21). Pre-drug well-being: significant for all subjective scales except bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, with effects more pronounced at higher well-being by the Discussion's summary; pre-drug anxiety: more 5D-ASC anxiety; openness: mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion: visual and auditory changes; previous hallucinogen experience: smaller 5D-ASC total, less anxious ego dissolution; lower CYP2D6 genetic activity score: higher plasma LSD and more anxious ego dissolution; age more and body weight less bad drug effect; women smaller increases in four positive ratings (not significant in the one-dose sensitivity analysis) and in temperature (not reported there).

statement: In people who had used LSD in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (13,769 respondents reported past-year use: 63.9% were under 25, 79.6% men, and most lived in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), 102 of the 10,293 who answered the question (1.0%; about 1 in 100, or 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after LSD in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (75% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 10,293 as the past-year group. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, nothing that was taken was tested, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 102 people by an estimated 53,627 days of use (a mean of 5.21 days a year), the authors put the figure at 0.2% of past-year uses, which they call an underestimate because each person is counted once. In the companion analysis of the same survey, 19 of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after them, a share the authors describe as about five times lower (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). Saying yes was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% against 0.7%; χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001), among younger people (median age 21 against 22; p = 0.003) and among those with more days of use in the past year (median 3 against 2; p = 0.029), in separate tests without adjustment, and it did not differ by sex or by first use in the past year. Of the 102, most ticked anxiety or panic (71) and confusion (66), and many paranoia (50) or seeing or hearing things (46); 21 (20.6%) ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 (16.7%) an accident or trauma, 13 (12.7%) seizures and 12 (11.8%) passing out, none of it verified, and the authors say it is unknown which symptoms came from LSD and which from other drugs taken. 54.5% said they had been admitted to hospital, a share the authors call surprising and print without a count, noting that the survey did not define admission. The paper gives recovery as percentages without a denominator, 59.2% back to normal within 24 hours and 11.2% with consequences lasting beyond 4 weeks; both fit 98 respondents, and the editors' reading of the figure, which prints no values, gives 58 of 98 back to normal within 24 hours, 40 taking longer, 17 not back to normal after 5 to 7 days and 11 with problems beyond 4 weeks, 6 of whom said they had not recovered (the abstract gives the 11). In the session that led to emergency treatment, 33 of the 102 had taken nothing else and 69 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (51) or alcohol (24); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, 53.9% named the setting, 50.0% their mindset, 40.2% taking too much and 34.3% mixing with other drugs; about 13 of the 102 thought the drug had not been LSD and about 10 did not know (both read by the editors from a figure that prints no values). Afterwards, 62.7% said they had cut down their LSD use and 16.7% that it had not changed. The authors cite similar shares in later rounds of the same survey (0.9%, 1.0% and 0.8% in the 2019, 2020 and 2021 rounds; those reports were not read here); they write that the incidents captured are likely only a proportion of LSD-related adverse events, most likely the more severe ones, that some serious reactions may not lead to emergency treatment (for example from fear of legal consequences), that some visits may be false alarms raised by others, and that drugs mistaken for LSD, such as NBOMes, may account for some incidents. They read their results as showing LSD to be relatively safe when used recreationally, with adverse reactions 'typically short-lived, self-limiting and psychological in nature', while their own figures show 40 of 98 taking longer than a day and 21 of 102 reporting thoughts or acts of self-harm; the survey cannot count deaths or people who could not or did not answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

statement: In US adults living in households, surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health from 2001 to 2004 (130,152 respondents, a randomly selected sample representing the civilian adult population not living in institutions; response rate 78%, and about 10% more excluded from the public data file; Krebs & Johansen, 2013; funded by the Research Council of Norway, no competing interests declared), having ever used LSD, psilocybin (magic mushrooms), mescaline or peyote (21,967 people, 13.4% weighted; of them, 80.1% had used LSD, 61.5% psilocybin and 37.8% mescaline or peyote), compared with never having used any of them (108,034 people), is associated with higher unadjusted rates of each of 20 past-year mental health indicators but, after adjustment, with no higher odds of any of them. Before adjustment every indicator was more common in people who had used these drugs, by about 1.8 to 3.2 times (editors' calculation from the weighted percentages; for example serious psychological distress 15.5% against 7.5%, inpatient mental health treatment 2.9% against 0.9%, symptoms of a major depressive episode 6.8% against 2.7% and of non-affective psychosis 4.4% against 1.8%), and these people also differed on every other factor measured (for example lifetime cannabis use 98.2% against 33.0%, cocaine 70.1% against 6.7%, an extremely stressful event 52.3% against 33.9%). After adjustment for age, sex, ethnicity, income, education, marital status, liking to take risks, a lifetime extremely stressful event and lifetime use of ten other kinds of drugs, the adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.7 to 1.1 (serious psychological distress 1.0, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.1; major depressive episode 1.0, 0.8 to 1.2; non-affective psychosis 0.8, 0.6 to 1.1; upper limits at most 1.6, for mania and agoraphobia), and none was higher for any of the drugs separately or for LSD use in the past year (1,220 people), although the past-year LSD estimates were imprecise (for example feeling a force inserting thoughts 1.7, 0.8 to 3.5). Some adjusted odds were lower (for example any of the drugs and feeling a force taking over the mind 0.7, 0.5 to 1.0; psilocybin and psychiatric medication 0.8, 0.7 to 0.9; LSD in the past year and serious psychological distress 0.7, 0.6 to 0.9), but no correction was made for the 120 adjusted estimates in the tables and the further stratified models (editors' count), and the authors say some weak associations are likely due to chance. Everything was self-reported in a private computer interview: drug use as ever having used, with no analysis of how often or how much, and mental health as screening questions about the past year (the treatment items included treatment for alcohol or drug problems). The survey asked once, with no measures from before people first used these drugs, so it cannot show whether they cause, prevent or do not affect mental health problems; in the editors' reading, the absence of a difference depends on adjusting for other drug use, stressful events and risk-taking, some of which may have followed psychedelic use; and people in prisons, hospitals or the military were not sampled. The authors' statement that their findings do not support flashbacks or hallucinogen persisting perception disorder rests, for visual symptoms, on one item, having seen a vision others could not in the past year (probably asked only in 2001 and 2002, so answered by about two thirds of the respondents; adjusted odds ratio 1.0, 0.7 to 1.3; for past-year LSD 1.3, 0.8 to 2.1), which cannot identify a rare lasting condition. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a big US survey of 130,152 adults from 2001 to 2004, the 21,967 who had ever used LSD, magic mushrooms (psilocybin), mescaline or peyote reported each of 20 kinds of mental health problems asked about roughly 2 to 3 times as often as people who had never used them. But they had also used far more other drugs, taken more risks and lived through more extremely stressful events; once these and other differences were taken into account, none of the 20 was more common, and a few were less common, which may be chance. Everything was self-reported, and the survey asked people once, so it cannot show whether these drugs cause, prevent or do nothing to mental health problems; its one question about seeing things others could not cannot rule out rare lasting vision problems.

statement: In people studied from 1967 to 1970, both people given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings and people who had used illicit drugs sold as LSD, the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD, compared with no LSD or with each person's own sample from before LSD, changes chromosome breakage. Four of the primary studies have been read in full (Cohen et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969); the others, including every study of groups of people that reported raised breakage after LSD, are known only through one 1971 narrative review in Science (Dishotsky et al., 1971; figures second-hand; no search method or selection criteria stated; supported in part by the State of California Department of Mental Hygiene and by Mendocino State Hospital, where two of the authors worked; its tables include the authors' own unpublished study, and its second author, W. D. Loughman, was the first author of one of the negative studies, Loughman et al., 1967). What these studies measured was breaks seen under a microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells taken from the blood and made to divide in a culture dish, counted as breaks per cell in some studies and as the share of cells with any aberration in others, in groups of 1 to 46 people, by laboratories whose breakage rates in unexposed controls ranged from 0% to 11.9%; most breaks recorded were of a kind that the review's authors say mostly arises from the culture procedure itself, and they limit their own conclusion to damage detectable by the methods then available. The concern began with Cohen et al. (1967), as Tjio et al. (1969) note, mainly a study of cells in a dish, not of people: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors, whose results were pooled, was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 conditions of concentration and exposure time, against 0.037 (34 breaks in 925 cells) in untreated cultures from six people, with no statistical test of the difference (the review nonetheless lists it as significant) and, in the paper's own Table 1, no steady rise with concentration; its one patient, a man given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy who had also been treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, had 12% breakage in 200 cells 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7% of untreated cultures from other people, with no sample from before LSD. Two small cross-sectional studies found no excess: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent use of illicit LSD (7 of them also amphetamines), scored by someone who did not know their drug histories, against none in 112 cells from one concurrent control and 1 in 561 cells from 18 earlier controls of the same laboratory (Loughman et al., 1967); and 2.2 breaks per 100 cells (21 in 937) in 4 psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and 1.5 (14 in 914) in 4 patients given LSD in treatment, against 1.6 (15 in 950) in 4 hospital volunteers, with each sample cultured in two laboratories and blinding of the scorers not reported (Sparkes et al., 1968); groups this small cannot exclude a modest rise. The strongest study, Tjio et al. (1969), sampled 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis before and 1 to 10 days after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with coded samples scored by one reader who did not know whether a sample came before or after LSD: the share of cells with chromosome aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not a significant change (P = 0.3; 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 percentage points, editors' calculation); 3 patients had large rises (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%), and the 2 of them who could be retested were back within the normal range 71 and 229 days later (one still 2.32 points above his own earlier rate); there was no untreated comparison group, and 31 of the 32 had been given other medicines in hospital before their first sample. Cohen et al. and Tjio et al. both used LSD supplied by Sandoz Pharmaceuticals. What these designs can show is limited: cells in a dish are not people, blood cells are not sperm or egg cells (none of these studies examined those), and pharmaceutical LSD given in hospital is not street LSD of unknown content. In the review's tallies, of 310 people in 21 reports from 17 laboratories, at most 18 of 126 given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%) had breakage above their control group's average. The early reports of raised breakage in people, from 1967 on, came from three teams studying people who used many illicit drugs (80 of 86 people studied by two of them had raised rates; these reports are not yet read in full), whereas nine other teams studying similar people (88 people, editors' sum from Table 2, including those of Loughman et al. and Sparkes et al.) found none beyond that in the general population apart from one infant exposed before birth; nearly all of these people used other drugs too (of 77 with raised rates and detailed drug histories, 43 had used amphetamine), in one study 6 people who used other drugs but not LSD had breakage similar to 18 who used illicit LSD with other drugs (12.6% against 13.2%), and only 54% of 57 street samples sold as LSD contained it in relatively pure form. Among people given pharmaceutical LSD, the review's comparisons with unexposed controls found raised breakage in at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), all but one (Cohen et al.'s patient) reported by one team whose methods the review's authors criticize (as few as 3 of 61, 4.9%, leaving out that team's incomplete data); in 56 people tested before and after, 6 (10.7%) had raised breakage afterwards, 3 of them after LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968, as the review describes it) and 1 with a viral infection, and the review says the 5 of these 6 who were retested 2 weeks to 7.67 months later were back at their earlier rates (in Tjio et al.'s own figures, one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate); only the intravenous study (3 people) showed a significant group change (1.0% to 4.78%), and in Tjio et al.'s study, which the review counts as 37 patients, the 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before, reported with the 32 patients, went from 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from the paper's own Table 4, editors' calculation), not significantly. In cells exposed to LSD in a dish, 6 of 9 studies found more breaks, mostly at concentrations or exposure times the review's authors judge unreachable in people, and in one study aspirin raised breakage about as much as LSD (9.6% and 10.2% of cells, against 5.0% in untreated cells). On cancer, the review found no significant research, only three case reports of leukaemia or other cancers in about four years, and it says that, as of then, there appeared to be no definite evidence that LSD causes cancer. On birth defects, no malformation had been reported after pharmaceutical LSD and six after illicit LSD (several of the mothers also used other drugs), which the review's authors say may be coincidence; of 14 children exposed to illicit LSD before birth, 10 had raised breakage and all were healthy without birth defects; and in a series of 148 pregnancies, spontaneous abortions occurred in 37% when parents had used both pharmaceutical and illicit LSD, against 15% with pharmaceutical LSD alone and 20% in the general population, but only 12 of the pregnancies involved LSD during gestation and one woman accounted for 5 of the 10 abortions in the combined group. The best study tested 32 hospital patients before and after one dose of pure LSD, with slides read blind: cells with damaged chromosomes went from about 4 in 100 to about 6 in 100, a change that could be chance; 3 patients had big jumps, and the 2 retested months later were back in the normal range. risk_of_bias.note: Primary studies read in full: Tjio et al. (1969), coded samples scored blind before and after one dose, but no untreated comparison group, other medicines in 31 of 32 patients and infections between samples (card sc_tjio_1969, ROBINS-I serious); Loughman et al. (1967) and Sparkes et al. (1968), cross-sectional comparisons of 8 people against 19 controls and of 4 against 4, with groups differing in other drugs, age and psychiatric illness, illicit exposure self-reported and blinding of the scorers not reported in Sparkes et al. (ROBINS-E high); Cohen et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors with no statistical test, and one patient without a sample from before LSD (editors' checklist, high). The studies that reported raised breakage in groups of people are known only through the narrative review (card sc_dishotsky_1971: no search method or selection criteria; unpublished data, including the authors' own; its second author led Loughman et al., 1967) and cannot be appraised; as the review describes them they were small, with nearly universal use of other drugs, laboratories differing in methods, thresholds and control rates (0% to 11.9%), and no account of whether scorers knew which samples were exposed; one widely deviant value was excluded from a negative group.

inconsistency.note: Three teams reported raised breakage in people who used many illicit drugs sold as LSD, and LSD given into a vein raised it for a time in 3 people (both as the review describes them), whereas the studies read in full found no excess (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969, with 3 large rises among 32 patients), and most other teams in the review found none either. The explanation offered (other drugs, contaminated street drugs, infections, malnutrition, culture methods) is plausible but rests partly on one comparison of 6 with 18 people and on the authors' impressions, and the positive studies have not yet been read in full.

indirectness.note: Breaks seen under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture stand in for genetic harm in people; blood cells are not sperm or egg cells, which none of these studies examined (Tjio et al., 1969, p. 855); the cell study (Cohen et al., 1967) is not a study of people; hospital patients given pharmaceutical LSD, nearly all after other medicines, differ from people taking street LSD of unknown content; methods of 1967 to 1970; the studies that reported raised breakage in people are seen only second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Groups of 4 to 32 people in the primary studies read (1 to 46 in the review); in the largest study the 95% interval of the change, about −1.3 to +4.6 points from a starting 4.28% (editors' calculation from Tjio et al.'s Table 2), includes no change and a rise to about double; with 4 people per group only groups that do not overlap at all can differ significantly (Sparkes et al., 1968); the review's counts have no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review itself includes unpublished data.

grade.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies have now been read in full (Cohen et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3). The human primary studies are observational, two cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture study is preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after pharmaceutical LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies (8 people; groups of 4) found no excess but cannot exclude a modest rise; and the cell study where the concern began reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. The human studies that reported raised breakage (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen et al., 1967, in the New England Journal of Medicine; Hungerford et al., 1968) have been requested and are not yet read: they enter only as the review describes them, and reading them could change the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); and Cohen et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many street drugs and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.
